column6: From qaaqqusaq (“the summoned guest”) + the suffix -tsiaq (“beautiful, precious”), a term of address for a child named after a deceased relative.
Perhaps related to Afar qasá (“to be red”).
Borrowed from Arabic قيوم (qayyūm); compare Azerbaijani qəyyum (“guardian”).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كمال (Kemâl), from Arabic كَمَال (kamāl, “perfection, maturity”).
“Firm, strong, well-balanced”, from qendër (“center, middle”) + -ak (adjectival suffix).
Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish كریم (Kerîm), from Arabic كَرِيم (karīm).
From qivioq (“fluff, down”).
From qorxmaz (“fearless”). Compare Turkish Korkmaz.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek Κλεοπάτρα (Kleopátra).
Sino-Vietnamese word from 君 or 軍.
Feminine form of quartus (“the fourth”).

From Old French. The name of a third century French martyr, from Latin Quīntīnus, a derivative of the Roman praenomen Quīntus, from quīntus (“fifth”). It was brought to England by the Normans, but never became particularly popular. Compare Quinton.
Borrowed from Spanish Querubín, from querubín (“cherub”).
A Norman surname of Old French origin, from a place name Quincy or Quincey in France, ultimately from Latin Quintus (“fifth [born]”).
The surname is borrowed from Irish Ó Coinn (“descendant of Chief”).
Possibly from Doric Scots, quinne (young woman); though the name may also be a modern feminine version of Quinn.
Feminine form of the Roman gens name Quintus, from quintus (“the fifth”).
Probably blend of Quintus + Octavius.
A less common form of Quentin.
Derived from French Quentin, from Latin Quīntīnus, derivative of the Roman praenomen Quīntus, from quīntus (“fifth”) (used to distinguish the fifth-born child as per Roman naming conventions).
From Latin diminutive of Quīntus, from quīntus (“fifth”), itself from quīnque (“five”).
From Latin Quīntus, from Latin quīntus (“fifth”).
Variant of Quentin, merged with an Old English place name meaning "queen's town".
Borrowed from Latin Quīntus (“masculine praenomen”), from quīntus (“fifth”).
A diminutive of Paquito. From Paquito + -t and by rhyming.
Variant of Ciriaco, from Latin Cyriacus, from Koine Greek.
Derived from Latin Quirīnus, from Sabine Curēs, or adjective form of quirīs (“citizen”).
Borrowed from Latin Quiricus, from Ancient Greek Κυριακός (Kuriakós, “of the Lord”).
Swanton suggests a possible connection to kic (“woman”).
Shortened from names ending with -qulu, such as Allahqulu.
From one of the names for the snow bunting.
From one of the names for the snow bunting, Qulutaq + the name suffix -na.
From one of the names for the snow bunting, Qulutaq + endearing suffix -nnguaq.
From one of the names for the snow bunting.
Short form of Inequnaaq, inequnaq (“handsome, sweet”).
According to Prósper, from the monophthongization of earlier *kʷawrtos, itself dissimilated from *kʷaturtos, from Proto-Italic *kʷeturtos.
From one of the names for the snow bunting.
Sino-Vietnamese word from 貴 or 季.
Sino-Vietnamese word from 決 (“decide, determine”).
Metathesised form of Qərinə, from Arabic قَرِينَة (qarīna).
